hero.h1: Dashboard UX design that turns dense data into clear decisions
hero.sub: We design dashboards around the decisions users make, with the right hierarchy, drill-downs, and alerts, instead of every metric at once.

summary: Dashboards designed around the decisions users make, not every metric at once.
sourceContext: US UI/UX design agency; this page sells dashboard structure work (information architecture, decision workflows, alerts, role-based views) to data-heavy product teams.
abstract: Dashboard UX design structures the information hierarchy, decision workflows and alerts of a dashboard, so each user role sees the key performance indicators (KPIs) behind the decisions that role makes. Our dashboard UX design takes 4–8 weeks, costs $25,000–$60,000, and ends with tested role-based views and drill-down paths.

sections.answer: Dashboard UX design is the user experience (UX) design of a dashboard: the choice of metrics, the hierarchy of metrics and the path from a number to an action. Designers start from the decisions each role makes, for example approving orders or escalating incidents, and remove metrics no decision needs.
sections.body: Dashboard UX design sets the structure, and dashboard design services set the visual layer, for example chart styles and component kits. A KPI dashboard with a clear dashboard information architecture shows 5–7 metrics per view, with a drill-down path to the detail behind each metric.

sections.h2: What does dashboard UX design include?
sections.answer: Our dashboard UX design includes 6 deliverables: a decision inventory, a KPI map, a dashboard information architecture, role-based views, an alerting model and a tested prototype.

items.title: Decision inventory.
items.body: A list of the decisions each user role makes, for example daily stock reorders or weekly budget reviews.

items.title: KPI map.
items.body: Every metric linked to one decision and one data source, for example on-time delivery rate linked to the weekly carrier review.

items.title: Dashboard information architecture.
items.body: The hierarchy of overview, summary and detail levels, for example 1 overview screen with 3 drill-down levels.

items.title: Role-based views.
items.body: Separate views per role built on role-based access control, for example an executive view and an analyst view.

items.title: Alerting model.
items.body: Thresholds, alert states and notification rules, for example a red state when stock falls below 2 days of cover.

items.title: Tested prototype.
items.body: A clickable Figma prototype tested with 5 users per role, for example a 5-task decision test in Maze.

sections.h2: How does the dashboard UX design process work?
sections.answer: The dashboard UX design process takes 4–8 weeks (20–40 working days) and runs in 5 steps, from decision discovery to handoff.

items.title: Decision discovery (3–5 days)
items.body: We interview 5–8 users per role and list decisions, data sources and workarounds as Jobs to be Done.

items.title: KPI mapping and information architecture (5–10 days)
items.body: Designers map each KPI to a decision and structure the overview, summary and detail levels.

items.title: Workflows and alerts (5–10 days)
items.body: Designers wireframe drill-down paths, filters and alert states for each role-based view.

items.title: Prototype testing (5–10 days)
items.body: Users from each role complete 5 decision tasks in a Figma prototype, and designers fix every failed task.

items.title: Handoff (2–5 days)
items.body: We hand over the information architecture, annotated wireframes and alert rules to the visual design and engineering teams.

sections.h2: What are the benefits of dashboard UX design?
sections.answer: Dashboard UX design has 4 benefits: it increases dashboard adoption, improves decision-making, reduces time to find data and develops shared KPI definitions.

items.title: Increases dashboard adoption
items.body: Views built around each role's decisions increase the share of users who open the dashboard every week.

items.title: Improves decision-making
items.body: A clear information hierarchy puts the metric behind each decision first, so users act on the right number.

items.title: Reduces time to find data
items.body: Drill-down paths and saved filters reduce the clicks between an alert and the record behind the alert.

items.title: Develops shared KPI definitions
items.body: The KPI map develops one definition per metric across product, operations and finance teams.

sections.h2: Dashboard UX design vs dashboard design services
sections.answer: Dashboard UX design decides what a dashboard shows and for whom; dashboard design services decide how the dashboard looks and how developers build the dashboard. Most teams run dashboard UX design first.

sections.h2: How much does dashboard UX design cost?
sections.answer: Dashboard UX design costs $25,000–$60,000 and takes 4–8 weeks. The price depends on 4 factors: the number of user roles, the number of KPIs, the number of data sources and the number of test rounds.
sections.body: A single-role KPI dashboard with 10–15 metrics and 1 test round sits near $25,000. A multi-role operations dashboard with 4 role-based views, an alerting model and 3 test rounds sits near $60,000. Dashboards inside a larger product continue with web app design services.

sections.h2: When does an operations team need dashboard UX design?
sections.answer: An operations team needs dashboard UX design in 5 situations:
items: Users export dashboard data to spreadsheets, if the dashboard does not answer daily questions.
Several roles share one dashboard, if executives and analysts need different levels of detail.
Operators ignore alerts, if every alert has the same priority.
A business intelligence (BI) rollout starts, for example a move to Power BI, Tableau or Looker.
Teams report different numbers for the same KPI, if metric definitions live in separate spreadsheets.

sections.answer: These answers cover the 5 questions buyers ask most about dashboard UX design.

faqs.q: Is dashboard UX design the same as dashboard visual design?
faqs.a: No. Dashboard UX design sets metrics, hierarchy and workflows, while dashboard visual design sets colours, chart styles and components.

faqs.q: Do you design dashboards for Power BI, Tableau or Looker?
faqs.a: Yes. Dashboard UX design works for Power BI, Tableau and Looker dashboards, and for custom dashboards built in code.

faqs.q: Does dashboard UX design include alerts?
faqs.a: Yes. Dashboard UX design includes an alerting model with thresholds, alert states and notification rules for each user role.

faqs.q: Should every user role see the same dashboard?
faqs.a: No. Every user role needs a role-based view, because an executive and an analyst make different decisions with different metrics.

faqs.q: How long does dashboard UX design take?
faqs.a: Dashboard UX design takes 4–8 weeks, which equals 20–40 working days, from decision discovery to handoff.
